passages.t: The bush that burns and is not burned up
passages.happening:
“Meanwhile, Moses was shepherding the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God” (verse 1).

“There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blazing fire from within a bush. Moses saw the bush ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed” (verse 2). Moses says, “I must go over and see this marvelous sight. Why is the bush not burning up?” (verse 3).

God calls to him from the bush, “Moses, Moses!” and he answers, “Here I am” (verse 4). “Do not come any closer,” God says. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground” (verse 5).

“I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And “Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Moses has spent long years keeping sheep in Midian. Stephen counts forty (Acts 7:30). Shepherding was humble work. The man raised in Pharaoh's palace now tends another man's flock, as Jacob once tended Laban's.

Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai. Deuteronomy mostly says Horeb; Exodus mostly says Sinai. Where it is has never been settled. Christian tradition since the fourth century has placed it at Jebel Musa in the south of the Sinai Peninsula. Early in the 380s a pilgrim named Egeria described a church standing beside a bush in a garden at the foot of that mountain, and the emperor Justinian later built a monastery around the spot. Others propose peaks in the north of the peninsula, or in northwest Arabia, the land of Midian. The book page sets out these views. The text calls it simply ‘the mountain of God’.

The ‘angel of the LORD’ appears, and then God himself speaks, with no break between them. ‘Angel’ means messenger. Here the messenger speaks and acts for God so fully that meeting him is meeting God. Some early Christian writers, beginning with Justin Martyr in the second century, took this angel as the Son of God appearing before he was born as a man. Others take him as a created messenger who speaks in God's name. The text stresses that in meeting the angel, Moses met God.

Moses comes to look at a wonder, and finds that he is the one being looked at. The Hebrew uses the word ‘see’ again and again in these verses. The word for this kind of thornbush is rare, and it sounds like ‘Sinai’. The fire in the bush looks ahead to the fire on the mountain in chapter 19. A Jewish teacher in an old commentary said God spoke from a lowly thornbush to show that no place is empty of his presence.

Taking off sandals was a sign of reverence, and of a servant's place before a master. The ground was holy not because of the place, but because God was there. This is the first time the Bible uses the word ‘holy’ of a place.

God introduces himself as the God of Moses' father, and of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. This is no new god. It is the God of Genesis, the God of the promises. Moses hides his face, because he believes no one can see God and live.
passages.later:
Joshua hears the same words before the commander of the LORD's army: “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy” (Joshua 5:15). Later in Exodus God tells Moses, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20). And Moses calls God “Him who dwelt in the burning bush” (Deuteronomy 33:16).

Jesus uses this very verse to answer those who denied the resurrection. He asks if they have read “about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’” (Mark 12:26). Then he says, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark 12:27). A God who binds his name to Abraham long after Abraham's death will not let death end that bond.
passages.asks: Moses turned aside to look, and found himself looked at by God. Ask what it would mean for you to turn aside from your ordinary work to pay attention to God. And ask what ‘holy ground’ might be in your own life, a place or a time where you need to come with reverence.

passages.t: God has seen, and has come down
passages.happening:
“The LORD said, ‘I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors, and I am aware of their sufferings. I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey’” (verses 7-8).

“And now the cry of the Israelites has reached Me, and I have seen how severely the Egyptians are oppressing them” (verse 9).

“Therefore, go! I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people the Israelites out of Egypt” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This is God's answer to the end of chapter 2. There God heard, remembered, saw and knew. Now he says it himself: I have seen, I have heard, I am aware. The Hebrew for ‘I have indeed seen’ says, word for word, seeing, I have seen: a way of saying it with force.

Notice the words God uses: ‘My people’. Israel has been Pharaoh's slaves. God calls them his own.

‘Affliction’ comes from the same Hebrew word as the oppression of 1:11. God names what Egypt did to them. He does not soften it.

Then come the verbs of action: ‘I have come down to rescue them’. And then the surprise: ‘I am sending you’. The rescue is wholly God's act, and yet it will be carried out by a man. That man had once tried to rescue his people on his own and failed (2:11-15). Now God sends him.

‘A land flowing with milk and honey’ is said about twenty times in the Old Testament. It means rich pasture for goats and sheep, and plenty of sweetness. The Hebrew word for honey can mean honey from bees or syrup from dates or grapes. An old Egyptian tale, the Story of Sinuhe, praises a land in the same region for its figs, grapes, honey, olives and cattle in very similar words.

The list of peoples in verse 8 is the Bible's usual way of naming those who lived in Canaan. The ‘Hittites’ here are probably groups in Canaan known by that name, not the great Hittite empire far to the north.
passages.later:
Stephen tells this scene in Acts: “I have indeed seen the oppression of My people in Egypt. I have heard their groaning and have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you back to Egypt” (Acts 7:34).

Joseph had promised it: “God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Genesis 50:24).

Isaiah remembers the exodus in words of great tenderness: “In all their distress, He too was afflicted, and the Angel of His Presence saved them” (Isaiah 63:9). Christians see the same movement, a God who sees and comes down, completed when the Son came from heaven to save.
passages.asks: God says, ‘I have seen’ and ‘I have heard’. Ask what suffering of your own, or of others, you need to believe God sees. And ask whether God might be sending you, as he sent Moses, to be part of his answer to someone's cry.

passages.t: ‘Who am I?’ ‘I will surely be with you’
passages.happening:
“But Moses asked God, ‘Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?’” (verse 11).

“‘I will surely be with you,’ God said, ‘and this will be the sign to you that I have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, all of you will worship God on this mountain’” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is the first of five objections Moses will raise (3:11; 3:13; 4:1; 4:10; 4:13). Calls of God in the Bible often follow a pattern: God meets someone, gives a task, hears an objection, gives a promise and a sign. Gideon (Judges 6) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1) are called in the same way. Moses stretches the pattern almost to breaking. He keeps objecting.

‘Who am I?’ In Hebrew the question uses the word for ‘I’. God does not answer by praising Moses, or by telling him how gifted he is. He answers with himself: ‘I will surely be with you’. The Hebrew word is ehyeh, ‘I will be’. Two verses later that same word becomes God's name.

The sign is strange. Most signs come before, to give courage. This one comes after. When the people have come out, they will worship God on this very mountain. Moses must go first, and the proof will follow. It is a sign that has to be trusted before it can be seen.
passages.later:
God answers Gideon's doubt the same way: “I will be with you” (Judges 6:16). And God tells Jeremiah, who says he is too young, “for I am with you to deliver you” (Jeremiah 1:8).

Jesus ends Matthew's Gospel with the same kind of promise to those he sends: “surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).
passages.asks: Moses asked, ‘Who am I?’ and God answered, ‘I will be with you’. Ask what task you feel too small for. Then ask whether your question has really been about you, when God's answer is about himself.

passages.happening:
Moses asks: if the people ask, “‘What is His name?’ What should I tell them?” (verse 13).

“God said to Moses, ‘I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’’” (verse 14).

God also tells him to say that “The LORD, the God of your fathers” has sent him. “This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world a name told who someone was, and made it possible to call on them. Some peoples believed that to know a god's secret name was to have power over that god. An Egyptian story tells how the goddess Isis tricked the sun god Ra into telling her his secret name, so that she could share his power. Moses' question asks more than a word. It asks what this God will prove to be.

God's answer, ‘I AM WHO I AM’, is in Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh. It is built from the verb ‘to be’. Because the Hebrew verb covers present and future, it can also be translated with the future: I will be what I will be. Many English Bibles put that in a footnote. The ancient Greek translation said, I am the one who is. Two other ancient Jewish translators, Aquila and Theodotion, used the future, closer to the Hebrew form.

Then God gives the name itself, ‘the LORD’. In Hebrew it is four letters, YHWH, probably said ‘Yahweh’. It sounds like ‘he is’ or ‘he will be’, the same verb as ‘I AM’. It is by far the most common name for God in the Old Testament, about 6,800 times. In time Jews stopped saying it aloud out of reverence and said Adonai, ‘Lord’, instead. Most English Bibles print it LORD in small capitals.

What does the name mean? Readers have heard three things, and they fit together. God simply is: he depends on nothing and no one. God is free: no one can define him or get hold of him, and he will be what he chooses to be. And God will be there: he will be with his people. The Talmud reads it as a promise that God will be with Israel in this slavery as in every later one. In this chapter the promise comes first, because the name is given to people in chains, two verses after God said, ‘I will surely be with you’.
passages.later:
God makes himself known by this name again in Exodus 6, and he proclaims what it means in Exodus 34:6: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness”.

Revelation calls God the one “who is and was and is to come” (Revelation 1:8), which many read as a fuller form of that Greek wording.

In John's Gospel Jesus says, “before Abraham was born, I am!” (John 8:58), and his hearers pick up stones, as if they heard him claim the divine name. Many readers hear Exodus 3 behind those words. Others note that the same Greek words also translate God's ‘I am he’ in Isaiah (Isaiah 43:10), so the echo may be of Isaiah as much as of Exodus.
passages.hard:
What does ‘I AM WHO I AM’ mean? Is it an answer, or a refusal to answer?

Some readers think God is partly refusing to be named on Moses' terms. A name, in that world, could be used to call up or control a god. God will not be handed over like that. He will be who he will be.

Others take it as a full answer about God's being. Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth century argued that ‘He Who Is’ is the most fitting name of God, because God does not borrow his existence from anything else. A medieval Jewish teacher, Maimonides, read it in a similar way, as pointing to God's necessary being.

Others, among them the Jewish scholar Martin Buber, read it mainly as a promise of presence: I will be there, as whoever I will be there. The context supports this, since the same word, ehyeh, was a promise in verse 12.

These readings do not cancel each other. A God who simply is, who cannot be controlled, and who promises to be with his people, is the God the rest of Exodus shows. The chapter leaves the name with some mystery in it, and that mystery is part of what it teaches. The book page says more about the name, and about how 6:3 fits with Genesis.
passages.asks: God's name is a promise: I will be there. Ask what it would change to pray to God as the one who is, and who will be with you. And ask whether you have been trying, in some way, to name God on your own terms, or to keep him where you can manage him.

passages.t: What will happen: the elders, Pharaoh, and Egypt's silver
passages.happening:
God tells Moses to gather Israel's elders and tell them, “I have surely attended to you and have seen what has been done to you in Egypt” (verse 16).

Then Moses and the elders are to go to Pharaoh and ask him to let them go three days into the wilderness, “so that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God” (verse 18). “But I know that the king of Egypt will not allow you to go unless a mighty hand compels him” (verse 19). God will strike Egypt with wonders, “And after that, he will release you” (verse 20).

“And I will grant this people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that when you leave, you will not go away empty-handed” (verse 21). Each woman is to ask her neighbor for silver and gold jewelry and clothing. “So you will plunder the Egyptians” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The elders were the heads of families and clans who spoke for the people. Even in slavery, Israel had kept them.

‘I have surely attended to you’ repeats almost exactly the words of Joseph's dying promise, ‘God will surely visit you’ (Genesis 50:24). The elders hear words their families had carried for generations.

Then God lays out the plan of the whole story in advance. The elders will listen (4:29-31). Pharaoh will refuse (chapter 5). God will stretch out his hand (chapters 7 to 12). And Israel will leave with Egypt's silver and gold (12:35-36).

Asking leave from work to make an offering to a god was a familiar kind of request in Egypt. An old record from a village of royal tomb-builders, from the fortieth year of Ramesses II, lists days when workers were away, some of them to make an offering to a god.

Verse 22's ‘ask’ is the plain Hebrew word for ‘ask’. Older English Bibles said ‘borrow’, which made it sound like a trick. The text never promises to give anything back. And verse 21 says the Egyptians give because God grants Israel favor in their eyes, not because they are fooled. The word ‘empty-handed’ in verse 21 is the same word Israel's law later uses for a freed slave, who must not be sent away with nothing.
passages.later:
The law gives the principle: when a slave is released, “do not send him away empty-handed” (Deuteronomy 15:13).

God had promised Abraham it would be so: “afterward they will depart with many possessions” (Genesis 15:14).

It happens just as God said: “the Israelites acted on Moses’ word and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing” (Exodus 12:35). The same gold later goes both into the golden calf (Exodus 32:2-4) and into the tabernacle (Exodus 35:22).
passages.hard:
Did God tell Moses to deceive Pharaoh with a three-day request, and to take Egypt's wealth? The charge is old. In the second century, Marcion, who rejected the God of the Old Testament, pointed to this passage as proof of a God who commands fraud.

On the wealth: the verb means ‘ask’, not ‘borrow’, and the Egyptians give willingly because of God's favor. The early Christian writers Irenaeus and Tertullian answered Marcion that the gifts were a small payment of wages for generations of unpaid labor. A Jewish legend in the Talmud makes the same point: when the Egyptians sue for their gold, Israel's advocate answers with a claim for the wages of all those years.

On the three days, readers differ. Many traditional Jewish commentators see a deliberately small first request that shows how hard Pharaoh's heart is, since God says at once that Pharaoh will refuse even this; as the plagues go on, the full demand becomes plain (10:8-11). Others accept that the request hides the whole plan, and judge it a fair way to deal with a tyrant who had ordered the murder of Israel's sons, like the midwives' answer in chapter 1. Readers who hold Scripture in high regard are found on both sides, and these notes take no side.
passages.asks: God promised that a people who had been robbed of their work would not leave with nothing. Ask what it means that God cares about fair wages and about what is owed to the poor. And ask whether there is anyone you owe something to, whom you have sent away empty-handed.
